title: Flow operators
scopeHtml: Scope: the intermediate-operator toolbox of Flow (transform, flattening, combining, rate limiting, accumulation, limiting, lifecycle hooks, custom operators) and how to assemble them into real pipelines. Notes on versions: kotlinx.coroutines 1.8-1.10; several operators here (debounce, sample, flatMapLatest, flatMapMerge, transformLatest) have carried @FlowPreview / @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi opt-in annotations, so check the annotation in the version you ship.

questions.promptHtml: What do map, filter, transform and onEach do on a Flow, and how do you choose between them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline fluency. Candidates who only know map/filter miss that transform is the primitive and that onEach is for side effects, not for changing data.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "map converts each item one-to-one, filter drops items by predicate, onEach runs a side effect and passes the same item downstream, and transform is the general one: it gets a collector receiver, so I can emit zero, one or many items per input, even before or after the item. map and filter are just thin wrappers over transform. All of them are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operator collects."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Every intermediate operator takes a Flow<T> and returns a new Flow<R> that wraps the upstream. The lambdas are suspend lambdas, so you can call suspend functions (a repository, delay) inside them without any adapter.

Operator Input -> output Typical use
map { } 1 -> exactly 1 DTO -> UI model
mapNotNull { } 1 -> 0 or 1 parse, drop failures
filter { } / filterNot 1 -> 0 or 1 (same item) drop invalid
filterIsInstance<R>() type narrowing sealed event streams
onEach { } 1 -> same item, side effect logging, analytics, caching
transform { } 1 -> N (0..n) expand, interleave a header, emit Loading then Result
withIndex() wraps in IndexedValue numbering

transform internally: the operator calls your block with the item and the downstream FlowCollector as receiver. map is literally transform { emit(mapper(it)) }.

Runtime facts that matter:

  • Operators run sequentially, in the collector's coroutine, one item at a time. Item 2 does not enter map until item 1 has gone through the entire downstream chain (no buffering unless you add buffer/flowOn).
  • An exception thrown in map terminates the flow and propagates downstream to catch / the collector.
  • onEach is not a terminal operator. flow.onEach { render(it) } does nothing until collected; launchIn(scope) is the usual way to collect it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ui: Flow<UiItem> = repo.orders()                 // Flow<List<OrderDto>>
    .map { list -> list.filter { it.isActive } }     // 1 -> 1
    .onEach { analytics.log("orders", it.size) }     // side effect only
    .transform { list ->                              // 1 -> N
        emit(UiItem.Header(list.size))
        list.forEach { emit(UiItem.Row(it)) }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using map for side effects and returning Unit/the same value; use onEach.
  • Doing heavy CPU work in map and assuming it is off the main thread. Operators run on the collector's dispatcher unless flowOn is used (see the flowOn chunk).
  • Emitting from a different coroutine inside transform (launch { emit(x) }) which breaks the flow invariants (IllegalStateException), see custom operator question.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between Flow.map and List.map? -> Flow's is lazy, suspending and per-collection; the list one is eager and creates a whole new list.
  2. How do you emit a Loading state before a network result? -> flow { emit(Loading); emit(Success(api.get())) } or onStart { emit(Loading) } on the data flow.
  3. Does onEach run if there is no collector? -> No. Flows are cold; nothing executes without a terminal operator.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the operators. The senior adds that transform is the primitive, that execution is sequential per item and runs on the collector's context, and that the suspend lambdas make operators a place where blocking or expensive work silently lands on Main.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A map { bitmapDecode(it) } in a ViewModel flow collected on Main caused jank because the operator inherited Main; the fix was flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) placed after the map.

questions.promptHtml: If I build a chain like flow.filter{}.map{}.distinctUntilChanged() and collect it twice, what runs, how many times, and where does the operator state live?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand operators as decorators over a cold producer, and why stateful operators are safe per collection.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each operator just builds a new Flow object that wraps the previous one; nothing executes at build time. Every terminal call re-runs the whole chain from the source, so two collectors means the producer runs twice. Stateful operators like distinctUntilChanged, take, scan keep their state in local variables inside the collect call, so each collection gets fresh state. The danger is state I capture myself outside the lambda."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
source flow{}  <-- filter wraps  <-- map wraps  <-- distinct wraps  <-- collect()
 collect() calls distinct.collect(c) -> map.collect(...) -> filter.collect(...) -> source block runs

Each collect call walks down to the source, and the source's block starts executing. Every stage has its own FlowCollector created for that particular collection. distinctUntilChanged for example does var previous = NULL inside collect, so a second collector starts with no previous value.

What does not get reset: anything you declared outside operator lambdas.

class Bad {
    private var seen = 0                       // shared, survives across collections, not thread-safe
    val flow = source.onEach { seen++ }.filter { seen > 1 } // second collector sees a "dirty" counter
}

To share one execution across collectors you must make it hot: shareIn / stateIn (covered in the SharedFlow/StateFlow chunks).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming val f = source.map { sideEffect() } calls sideEffect at declaration.
  • Creating the Flow in a getter (val x get() = repo.flow().map{}): each access builds a new pipeline (cheap) but also each collection re-executes the source (expensive).
  • Believing distinctUntilChanged remembers across collectors/resubscriptions. After resubscribe, the first item always passes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A screen rotates; the collector restarts; does distinctUntilChanged still suppress the last value? -> No, state died with the collection; the first value always goes through. If the upstream is stateIn, the current value is replayed.
  2. Are operators thread-safe? -> The operator chain for one collection runs sequentially; its state is confined to that collection as long as you don't capture shared mutable state.
  3. Why is a mutable initial passed to scan dangerous? -> It is created once at assembly time and reused by every collection (see scan question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "flows are lazy". The senior explains decoration, per-collection state, and identifies shared captured state as the actual bug source.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "counter of retries" kept in a field outside the flow made the second screen visit skip the retry UI, since the field survived while the flow restarted.

questions.promptHtml: How do distinctUntilChanged and distinctUntilChangedBy work, and what are their limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is used in every UI pipeline; the signal is whether you know it is only consecutive, equality-based, and redundant on StateFlow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It drops an item if it equals the previous emitted item (==). It is only consecutive de-duplication, not a global set. distinctUntilChangedBy { it.id } compares a derived key, and there is an overload taking a custom (old, new) -> Boolean. On a StateFlow it is pointless because StateFlow already de-duplicates by equality, and the stdlib marks it as having no effect."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
It stores the last emitted value in a local variable; for each incoming item, it checks areEquivalent(previous, new) and only emits when different (the first item always passes). Comparison uses equals, so data classes work well, while objects without equals compare by identity.

state
    .map { it.cart }                      // project first
    .distinctUntilChanged()               // then dedupe on the narrow slice
    .collect(render)

items.distinctUntilChangedBy { it.id }    // key-based
items.distinctUntilChanged { old, new -> old.version == new.version } // custom

Why project first? De-duping the whole state with a field that changes constantly (e.g., timestamp) defeats the dedupe; de-dupe the slice that the consumer cares about.

Limits: A, B, A is emitted three times (consecutive only). For global dedupe, keep a HashSet in the flow body (state per collection) and filter { seen.add(it) }; remember memory growth.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutating the same list instance and re-emitting it: old == new is trivially true (same reference) so the update is dropped (explored in a scenario in this chunk).
  • Putting distinctUntilChanged() before the map that narrows the value, so it dedupes nothing useful.
  • Adding it after stateIn: no effect, the warning is a hint.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it use hashCode? -> No, only equals (via ==) with the previous element.
  2. Why would two equal-looking items still pass? -> Missing equals (plain class), floating-point values, or arrays (identity equality).
  3. How would you dedupe by time window instead? -> That is not distinct; use debounce/sample/custom throttle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "removes duplicates". Senior: consecutive only, equality semantics, projection-before-dedupe, StateFlow redundancy, and the mutable-instance trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cart badge recomposed on every price tick because dedupe was applied on the whole CartState rather than on .map { it.count }.

questions.promptHtml: What do take, takeWhile, drop, dropWhile (and first()) do, and what happens to the upstream producer when you stop early?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The cancellation behavior of take is subtle: upstream is cancelled, finally blocks run, and hot flows are not "stopped".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "take(n) passes the first n items then completes the flow and cancels the upstream; takeWhile does the same when the predicate first fails (the failing item is not emitted); drop(n) skips the first n; dropWhile skips until the predicate first fails then passes everything. first() is effectively take(1) plus a terminal. Early completion is implemented by cancelling the upstream collection, so cleanup in finally or onCompletion runs."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
take(n) collects upstream and after emitting the n-th item it aborts the collection by throwing a private AbortFlowException (internal, never visible to you) which unwinds upstream, runs finally blocks, and is swallowed by take itself. It does not wait for the (n+1)-th upstream item, so take(1) on a slow flow completes right after the first emission. take(count) requires count > 0.

Hot sources: sharedFlow.take(1) stops your collection, not the shared producer. The SharedFlow keeps running for others.

val first3 = flow {
    try { var i = 0; while (true) emit(i++) }
    finally { println("producer cancelled") }   // prints after the 3rd item
}.take(3).toList()                              // [0, 1, 2]

val afterAuth = events.dropWhile { it !is Event.Authenticated } // skip pre-auth noise
val untilError = lines.takeWhile { it != "EOF" }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• onEach { sideEffect() }.take(3): the side effect runs 3 times; with take(3).onEach also 3, but position relative to expensive map decides if you compute item 4 (you do not, because upstream is cancelled right after item 3 is emitted).
  • Expecting takeWhile to include the first failing element (it does not).
  • Swallowing CancellationException in a producer's try/catch and thereby defeating the early stop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. take(1) vs first()? -> first() is a terminal returning the value (throws NoSuchElementException if empty); take(1) is an intermediate returning a Flow.
  2. Does take unsubscribe from a callbackFlow? -> Yes, awaitClose block runs, so you unregister the listener there.
  3. How do you take items for a duration? -> timeout/withTimeoutOrNull { flow.toList(list) } or a takeUntil(signalFlow) custom operator.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior sees slicing; senior knows it is cancellation-driven (AbortFlowException), that finally/awaitClose cleanup runs, and that hot producers continue.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A callbackFlow of GPS updates leaked the location listener because the awaitClose was missing; first() on it "worked" but the listener kept running.

questions.promptHtml: What are onStart, onEmpty and onCompletion for, and when does each fire?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lifecycle hooks are how you add Loading states and cleanup without touching the source; interviewers check whether you know they can emit and what the cause means.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "onStart runs before the upstream is collected and can emit, so it is where I emit Loading. onEmpty runs only if the upstream completes without emitting anything, and can emit a fallback. onCompletion runs on normal completion, failure or cancellation, with a nullable cause; it observes the failure but does not catch it, so catch is still needed."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• onStart { emit(x) }: action executes first, then the upstream collection starts. For a StateFlow the onStart emission appears before the current value. If the onStart block throws, upstream is never collected.
  • onEmpty { emit(default) }: fires when upstream completes normally with zero items. Not triggered on exception.
  • onCompletion { cause -> }: cause == null on normal completion; non-null with the exception on failure or CancellationException when cancelled. It can emit only when the flow is not cancelled/failed downstream in a way that prevents it, and the exception continues to propagate afterwards.

Order example: flow{emit(1)}.onStart{emit(0)}.onCompletion{emit(2)} -> 0, 1, 2.

repo.search(q)
    .map<List<Item>, UiState> { UiState.Content(it) }
    .onStart { emit(UiState.Loading) }
    .onEmpty { emit(UiState.Empty) }
    .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it)) }
    .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause is CancellationException) log("cancelled") }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting onStart { emit(Loading) } outside a flatMapLatest so Loading shows once, not per query; it belongs inside the inner flow.
  • Using onCompletion as finally for resources: it is fine, but the finally in the producer is closer to the resource.
  • Expecting onEmpty for an empty list: a Flow<List<T>> emitting emptyList() is not empty.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does onCompletion swallow errors? -> No; place catch after it or before depending on whether you want to observe.
  2. catch before or after onCompletion? -> catch first (upstream of it) means onCompletion sees null; catch after means onCompletion sees the exception.
  3. Can onCompletion run on cancellation and emit? -> It runs, but emitting from a cancelled coroutine fails; use withContext(NonCancellable) for suspending cleanup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "onStart for loading". Senior: placement relative to catch and flatMapLatest, cause semantics, and cancellation behavior.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A spinner never hid when the user left mid-request: the hide call lived only on the success path instead of onCompletion.

questions.promptHtml: Explain flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest. Give a use case for each and how their output differs for the same input.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The single most asked operator question. It reveals if you reason about concurrency and ordering of inner flows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "All three map each upstream item to an inner flow and flatten. flatMapConcat runs inner flows one at a time, preserving order. flatMapMerge runs up to N inner flows concurrently and emits in whatever order results arrive. flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow when a new upstream item arrives, so only the latest inner flow produces output. Concat for ordered writes, merge for parallel independent work, latest for search-as-you-type."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Take upstream 1, 2, 3 emitted 100 ms apart, with inner(n) = flow { emit("$n-a"); delay(250); emit("$n-b") }.

flatMapConcat : 1-a 1-b(t=250) 2-a 2-b 3-a 3-b          (total ~ 750ms+, sequential, ordered)
flatMapMerge  : 1-a 2-a 3-a  1-b 2-b 3-b                 (inners overlap; order by arrival)
flatMapLatest : 1-a 2-a 3-a 3-b                          (1 and 2 cancelled before their -b)

Mechanics:

  • flatMapConcat = map(transform).flattenConcat(). Upstream is not pulled for the next item until the current inner finishes: natural backpressure.
  • flatMapMerge(concurrency) launches each inner in a child coroutine, limited by a semaphore; see the concurrency question.
  • flatMapLatest = transformLatest { emitAll(transform(it)) }; each new item cancels the in-flight inner.
Ordering Parallelism Cancels old? Use for
Concat strict 1 no sequential writes, ordered pipeline
Merge arrival up to N no parallel fetches, independent items
Latest n/a 1 effective yes search, "current selection" detail loading

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
val detail = selectedId.flatMapLatest { id -> repo.observeDetail(id) }
val uploads = files.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 3) { f -> uploader.upload(f) }
val ordered = events.flatMapConcat { e -> sync.apply(e) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• flatMapLatest on operations that must complete (saving, payment). Cancelled mid-flight.
  • flatMapMerge with defaults on heavy work (default concurrency is 16).
  • Using flatMapConcat for a never-completing inner flow (e.g., Room observation) means later upstream items are never processed: the first inner flow never ends.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does flatMapConcat with a Room Flow as inner "freeze"? -> The inner never completes, so concat never moves on; use flatMapLatest.
  2. Is flatMapLatest safe with a network call? -> Yes if the call is cancellation-aware (Retrofit suspend functions, OkHttp calls cancel on coroutine cancellation).
  3. Exception in one inner flow of flatMapMerge? -> It cancels the others and fails the whole flow; catch inside the inner flow to isolate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: definitions plus "latest for search". Senior: picks by side-effect semantics (idempotent read vs write), knows concat deadlocks with infinite inners, and reasons about concurrency limits and error isolation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An outbox sync used flatMapLatest; rapid taps cancelled uploads mid-body and users saw duplicates after retry. It was changed to flatMapConcat with idempotency keys.

questions.promptHtml: Compare combine, zip and merge. When does each emit and complete, and which would you use to build a screen state from three sources?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Picking the wrong combiner is a classic bug (stuck loading, stale pairs). Tests emission and completion semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "merge interleaves several flows of the same type into one and completes when all complete. combine emits whenever any source emits, using the latest value of every other source, but only after each source has emitted at least once. zip pairs the n-th item of each flow with the n-th of the others and completes when the shortest completes. For screen state from several sources I use combine."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Marble with A: a1 ---- a2 ------, B: -- b1 -------- b2:

A:       a1(t1)      a2(t4)
B:             b1(t2)         b2(t6)
merge:   a1  b1  a2  b2                    (4 items)
combine: -   (a1,b1)@t2  (a2,b1)@t4  (a2,b2)@t6   (nothing at t1: B hasn't emitted)
zip:     (a1,b1)@t2  (a2,b2)@t6             (pairs by index; waits for the slower)

Details:

  • combine is conflating-ish: internally it uses channels and a latest-values array; if sources emit in rapid succession the transform may see only the latest combination, not every intermediate pair (it is not glitch-free).
  • zip backpressures the faster flow: it only proceeds as fast as the slower, so a 50 Hz and a 1 Hz source gives 1 Hz output with the fast side suspended/stale.
  • merge does not combine values; it needs a common supertype.
  • Completion: combine completes when all sources complete; zip as soon as one completes (the rest are cancelled); merge when all complete.
  • Failure in any source cancels the rest and fails the flow.
val state: Flow<ScreenState> = combine(user, cart, promos) { u, c, p ->
    ScreenState(u, c, p)
}
val allEvents = merge(clicks.map(::Click), swipes.map(::Swipe))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• zip for "state from two sources": output is tied to the slower, and drifts out of date.
  • Using combine with a source that never emits initially (stuck, see scenario).
  • Expecting combine to emit once for simultaneous source updates.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. combine vs flatMapLatest? -> combine joins independent streams; flatMapLatest switches one stream based on another's value (dependent).
  2. How to give a late source an initial value? -> onStart { emit(null) } or stateIn(initialValue).
  3. Is combine of StateFlows a StateFlow? -> No, a cold Flow; use stateIn (or combineStates helper from libraries) to get one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the definitions. Senior states the "after first emission of all" rule, completion differences, and the lack of glitch-freedom.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A profile page showed an infinite spinner for 6% of users who had no avatar: the avatar flow only emitted when an avatar existed, so combine never fired.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between debounce and sample? When would each be the wrong choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Both "reduce emissions", but one waits for silence and the other for a clock. Wrong choice causes starvation or wasted work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "debounce(t) emits an item only if no newer item arrives within t; it restarts its timer on every item, so a continuous stream never emits. sample(period) emits the most recent item once per period, regardless of activity, so it guarantees a steady rate. I use debounce for user typing, sample for high-frequency telemetry like sensors or scroll."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Items at t = 0, 100, 200, 300 then silence; debounce(150) vs sample(250):

input   : x0 x1 x2 x3 ............ (silence)
debounce(150): only x3 at t=450  (every gap before was < 150)
sample(250)  : x2 at t=250 (latest at tick), then nothing if no new item
  • debounce is time-since-last-item; the latency added is always the timeout; starvation is possible if the source never goes quiet for the timeout.
  • sample ticks on a fixed period (implemented with a ticker channel); emits only if there is a new value since the last tick. The last item that arrives after the last tick before upstream completion can be dropped (documented behavior), whereas debounce flushes the pending last value when upstream completes.
  • debounce { item -> timeoutMs } (lambda overload) lets the timeout depend on the value, e.g., 0 for empty query so clearing is instant. A Duration overload exists too.
  • Neither is a throttleFirst: the first item in a window is not emitted immediately by either (custom operator needed).
  • Both have shipped under @FlowPreview; check your version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@OptIn(FlowPreview::class)
val results = query
    .debounce { if (it.isEmpty()) 0L else 300L }
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest(repo::search)

val uiPos = scrollOffsetFlow.sample(100)      // at most 10 updates/s to the UI

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• debounce on a sensor/scroll stream: never fires (starvation).
  • sample for typing: user pauses mid-word, sample still fires on tick with a stale partial; also adds up to a full period of latency without saving requests.
  • Using either for button double-click protection where the first click should act immediately.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does debounce drop items? -> Yes, all but the last in each burst.
  2. Time in tests? -> They use delay internally so runTest virtual time works with advanceTimeBy.
  3. Which is cheaper on CPU? -> sample bounds work to 1/period, debounce bounds it to bursts; for a firehose sample is the one with guaranteed throughput.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "debounce for search, sample for sensors." Senior explains the starvation condition, completion-flush difference, value-dependent timeout and why neither replaces throttleFirst.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics scroll tracker on debounce(200) reported nothing for users who scrolled continuously; moving to sample(500) fixed the data.

questions.promptHtml: What do scan, runningFold and runningReduce do, and how would you use them to build a state reducer? What is the trap with the initial value?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: scan is the reducer primitive behind MVI-style state; the shared-mutable-initial trap shows depth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "scan(initial) { acc, v -> } emits the initial value first, then every intermediate accumulation. runningFold is the same operation under the collection-style name. runningReduce has no initial; its first output is the first element. For a state reducer I do events.scan(initialState, ::reduce). The trap: the initial value object is created once at assembly time, so a mutable initial is shared across collections."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Input 1,2,3:

scan(0){a,b->a+b}        : 0, 1, 3, 6      (initial emitted before any input)
runningReduce{a,b->a+b}  : 1, 3, 6
fold(0){...} (terminal)  : 6               (only final)

The accumulator lives in a local var inside the collect call, so each collection starts from initial again, which is right for immutable values. If initial is mutableListOf() and you mutate it in the lambda, then collection 2 starts with collection 1's leftover contents.

sealed interface Intent { object Inc : Intent; data class Set(val v: Int) : Intent }
data class State(val n: Int = 0)

fun reduce(s: State, i: Intent) = when (i) {
    Intent.Inc -> s.copy(n = s.n + 1)
    is Intent.Set -> s.copy(n = i.v)
}
val state: Flow<State> = intents.scan(State(), ::reduce)       // emits State() first

// Bug: shared mutable initial
val bad = pages.scan(mutableListOf<Item>()) { acc, p -> acc.apply { addAll(p) } }
// Good: immutable, copy per step (O(n) each, fine for small, think twice for 10k items)
val good = pages.scan(emptyList<Item>()) { acc, p -> acc + p }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the initial emission (UI renders initial state once, then again on the first event), or being surprised that scan emits with zero upstream items.
  • Mutable accumulator shared across collectors / config-change resubscribes.
  • O(n^2) copying when accumulating large lists per page; consider a persistent structure or Paging.
  • Side effects in the reducer: it must be pure for replay and tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. scan vs fold? -> fold is terminal and returns only the final value; scan is intermediate and emits every step.
  2. How do you make the scanned state survive recollection? -> stateIn/shareIn so one scan runs once and replays; otherwise each collector restarts from initial.
  3. Reducer needs suspend work? -> Use scan only for pure reduction; for async effects use flatMapConcat/transform with a state holder, or a Channel-based loop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows scan accumulates. Senior knows the initial-first emission, mutable-initial sharing, purity requirements and copy cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat screen accumulated messages using scan(mutableListOf()); after navigating back, old messages from the previous collection reappeared.

questions.promptHtml: combine has typed overloads only up to five flows. How do you combine seven flows, or a dynamic list of flows, and what are the pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real screens combine many sources. Tests API knowledge and the edge cases (empty list, type erasure, glitches).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Typed overloads go up to 5. Beyond that I use the combine(vararg flows) or combine(Iterable<Flow<T>>) overload whose transform receives an Array<T>, which means casting, or I nest: combine(combine(a,b,c){...}, combine(d,e,f){...}) {...} into small intermediate models. Pitfalls: an empty list completes immediately without emitting, the array overload needs a common supertype, and combine waits for every source to emit once."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// 1) Array overload (vararg is reified inline, transform gets Array<T>)
val state = combine(f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7) { arr ->
    Screen(arr[0] as User, arr[1] as Cart, /* ... unchecked casts */)
}

// 2) Dynamic list
val total = combine(listOfFlows) { values: Array<Int> -> values.sum() }

// 3) Nesting into cohesive sub-models (preferred)
val header = combine(user, avatar, badge) { u, a, b -> Header(u, a, b) }
val body   = combine(cart, promos, shipping, taxes) { c, p, s, t -> Body(c, p, s, t) }
val screen = combine(header, body) { h, b -> Screen(h, b) }

Nesting wins on type safety and readability, and the intermediate models are natural testing seams. It also reduces recomposition: header can use distinctUntilChanged independently.

Edge cases:

  • combine(emptyList<Flow<Int>>()) {} produces a flow that completes immediately with no emission. If "no inputs" should mean an empty result, guard: if (flows.isEmpty()) flowOf(emptyList()).
  • Mixed types with the vararg form degrade to Array<Any?>, with unchecked casts that fail at runtime if you reorder arguments.
  • All sources must emit once before the first emission; add onStart { emit(default) } to slow ones.
  • Every emission of any source recomputes everything. Expensive transforms should be cheap, or split with nesting.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reordering flows and forgetting to update array indices; the compiler cannot catch it.
  • Combining 7 StateFlows and then wondering why .value is not available (result is a cold Flow).
  • Expecting every intermediate combination during rapid updates; combine may collapse them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not zip for this? -> It pairs by index and tracks the slowest source.
  2. How do you keep it a StateFlow? -> stateIn(scope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial).
  3. Alternative to many combines? -> One state holder (MutableStateFlow<ScreenState> with update {}) fed by independent collectors, which avoids a combine wall and lets partial data render immediately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE finds the vararg overload. Senior prefers nested sub-model combines or a single state holder and calls out empty-list, cast, and first-emission pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen's 8-way combine array cast crashed with ClassCastException after someone inserted a flow in the middle; nesting into typed sub-models removed the class of bug.

questions.promptHtml: Does the order of operators in a Flow chain matter? Give concrete examples where swapping two operators changes behavior or cost.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reveals whether you think of a chain as a data-flow pipeline with cost and semantics at each stage.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Yes, constantly. Cheap, selective operators go first (filter, take) so expensive ones see fewer items. distinctUntilChanged goes after the projection it should compare. debounce goes before flatMapLatest so I don't start a request per keystroke. catch only handles errors from upstream of it, and onStart/flowOn apply to what is above them. Same operators, different order, different result."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Examples:

Chain Effect
filter{cheap}.map{expensive} vs reverse expensive runs on every item vs only on kept ones
map{it.count}.distinctUntilChanged() vs distinctUntilChanged().map{} first dedupes the slice; second dedupes the whole object (rarely equal)
take(3).map{} vs map{}.take(3) same output, but second may compute one extra mapping depending on position of side effects; with onEach before take, upstream effect for item 3 occurs either way, item 4 never
debounce(300).flatMapLatest{api} vs reverse requests per keystroke vs per pause
catch{} placed before vs after flatMapLatest error ends the whole pipeline or just the inner request
onStart{emit(Loading)} before/after flatMapLatest Loading once vs per inner flow
flowOn(IO) placement affects only operators above it (see flowOn chunk)
scan then distinctUntilChanged vs reverse dedupe states vs dedupe inputs (the latter changes the reduction!)

A mental model: read the chain top to bottom as stages on a conveyor belt; each stage should reduce volume or cost before the next.

val good = events
    .filterIsInstance<Event.Query>()        // cheap, narrows type
    .map { it.text.trim() }                 // cheap
    .filter { it.length >= 2 }              // shrinks volume
    .debounce(300)                          // time-based shrink
    .distinctUntilChanged()                 // dedupe on final key
    .flatMapLatest { repo.search(it).catch { emit(emptyList()) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• distinctUntilChanged before scan silently drops repeated inputs that were meaningful (two "Inc" events).
  • catch at the end swallowing and terminating everything.
  • Logging with onEach at the wrong place and being misled about what reaches the UI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you put flowOn? -> Right after the upstream operators that must run off-main, before the collector-side ones.
  2. Does operator order change thread? -> Only through flowOn/buffer boundaries, not otherwise.
  3. How do you debug a pipeline? -> Temporary onEach { Log } between stages, or .onEach + .also in a test with Turbine.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "order matters, e.g., debounce before flatMapLatest." Senior reasons about volume/cost reduction, semantic traps (scan vs distinct) and error scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A list screen mapped 5,000 rows through a mapper before filtering to 50 visible rows; swapping the order cut the mapper time from ~120 ms to ~2 ms per refresh.

questions.contextHtml: A profile screen (DAU 400k) builds its state with combine(userFlow, avatarFlow, badgesFlow) { u, a, b -> ProfileState(u, a, b) } collected via stateIn in the ViewModel. After a release, support reports "profile loading forever", about 6% of sessions, concentrated on new accounts. No crashes, no ANRs, Crashlytics clean. avatarFlow is a callbackFlow over an SDK listener that only invokes the callback when an avatar file exists. Backend latency p95 is normal. The release also bumped the Compose BOM and changed the image loader (red herrings).
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause, fix it for users now, and prevent the class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Compose or the image loader, adds a timeout to the screen, or sprinkles delays. Does not look at emission semantics of combine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it only new accounts? (hints at missing data). Did avatarFlow change in this release? Does the loading state derive from stateIn initial value? Can we reproduce with a fresh install and no avatar? Is the spinner tied to ProfileState or to a separate flag?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a server-driven flag or hotfix that gives avatarFlow a default null; meanwhile show the profile without the avatar via fallback to cached state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) combine never emits because avatar never emits for users without one; (b) stateIn initial Loading persists; (c) backend slow (ruled out by p95); (d) Compose recomposition issue (no evidence).
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a unit test with Turbine: combine(flowOf(user), emptyFlow/never(), flowOf(badges)) and assert no item within a time window; add a log in the transform; Android Studio debugger breakpoint in the transform on a fresh account, never hit.
  5. Root cause: combine emits only after every source has emitted at least once. With no avatar, the callbackFlow never emits, so combine never fires, and the state stays at its Loading initial value. If the source had completed without emitting, combine would complete silently, with the same visible symptom.
  6. Fix: short-term: avatarFlow.onStart { emit(null) } (or .map<Avatar?> + onStart). Long-term: model the optional source as Flow<Avatar?> that always emits a value, and make the SDK wrapper emit null on "no avatar" in the callback.
val avatar: Flow<Avatar?> = avatarFlow.map<Avatar, Avatar?> { it }.onStart { emit(null) }
val state = combine(userFlow, avatar, badgesFlow) { u, a, b -> ProfileState(u, a, b) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileState.Loading)
  1. Prevention: Contract test for every source passed to combine: "emits at least once". Lint/review checklist: each combined flow has an initial emission. Turbine test for "no data" cases; add a screen-level metric: time from open to first non-loading state, alert at p95 > 5 s.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global timeout that shows "error" (hides the bug). Not replacing combine by zip: it would wait for the same thing. onStart { emit(null) } can briefly flash the placeholder avatar before the real one: acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if one source throws? -> combine cancels all and the pipeline fails; catch per-source and map to a fallback value.
  • What if avatar emits first and user takes 3 s? -> Nothing renders until all emitted; consider rendering partial state from a single state holder.
  • Could onStart emit null after the real value on resubscribe? -> No, onStart runs before upstream is collected, so null is first, then the real value.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settings screen sat on a spinner for users who had never granted a permission because the permission-status flow only emitted on change. The team had a 3-line fix but the real lesson was a "must emit initial" convention for every combine input.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames UI libs, cannot explain combine semantics.
  • Hire: identifies the first-emission rule and fixes with onStart.
  • Strong hire: also adds contract tests, partial-render design, a metric on time-to-content, and discusses completion-without-emission.

questions.contextHtml:
Search-as-you-type for a marketplace app (1.2M DAU). After shipping, QA reports "search works until I type something that makes the server return a 500, then it never works again until I leave the screen". Crashlytics shows nothing. Here is the ViewModel code:

class SearchVm(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    val query = MutableStateFlow("")
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = query
        .debounce(300)
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .flatMapLatest { q -> repo.search(q).map { UiState.Content(it) } }
        .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it.message)) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Idle)
}

repo.search is a flow {} that throws HttpException on 500. Backend 5xx rate is about 0.3%. Red herring: someone suspects debounce is broken.
questions.promptHtml: Why does search die permanently after one error, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retry()" or "wrap in try/catch in the ViewModel", missing that catch is placed after the whole pipeline so the pipeline terminates.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the UI show the error once and then ignore typing? Is the failure always after a server error? Is the StateFlow still subscribed (screen alive)? Does repo.search throw or return a Result?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: move catch inside flatMapLatest. Backend errors no longer brick the screen.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Exception propagated through flatMapLatest terminated the outer flow; (b) stateIn job completed so no more upstream; (c) debounce bug (unlikely); (d) VM scope cancelled (no).
  4. How I'd verify each: Turbine test: query emits "a" (error) then "b", assert second result arrives. Log onCompletion { cause -> } before stateIn: it fires after the first error. Debug agent / breakpoints.
  5. Root cause: catch is an upstream-only operator: it catches the exception, emits the error state and then the flow completes, because exception caught means the upstream is already dead. Everything upstream (debounce, query collection) has been cancelled. stateIn keeps the last value (Error) but is no longer collecting query. Typing changes query, nobody listens.
  6. Fix: put the catch on the inner flow so only one request fails:
.flatMapLatest { q ->
    repo.search(q)
        .map<List<Item>, UiState> { UiState.Content(it) }
        .onStart { emit(UiState.Loading) }
        .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it.message)) }
}

Long-term: have the repository return a sealed Result/Either so expected failures are values, and let only genuine bugs throw. 7. Prevention: Turbine tests "error then recovery" for every long-lived pipeline. Review rule: catch goes at the innermost flow that may fail. Add onCompletion logging in debug to catch unexpected terminations. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not retry() at the end (re-subscribes the whole pipeline, can loop hot on a persistent error). Not try/catch around collect in the VM (same termination). retryWhen with backoff is right for transient inner errors only, not for 4xx.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the exception comes from distinctUntilChanged? -> Practically impossible; but any upstream exception kills the pipeline, so keep upstream operators total.
  • Does catch catch exceptions thrown in the collector? -> No, only upstream (exception transparency).
  • Would CancellationException hit catch? -> catch ignores cancellation of the collecting coroutine; do not treat it as an error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "live prices" ticker froze after the first malformed payload; the team had one catch at the end. The post-mortem standard became "catch at the boundary of each unit of work".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests retry or ignores operator scope.
  • Hire: moves catch inside flatMapLatest and explains termination.
  • Strong hire: adds Turbine recovery tests, Result-typed repository, and warns against global retry loops.

questions.contextHtml:
A to-do app (350k DAU) migrated from LiveData to Flow. After the migration, users report "I add an item and the list does not update until I rotate the phone". The ViewModel:

class TodoVm : ViewModel() {
    private val items = mutableListOf<Todo>()
    private val _list = MutableStateFlow<List<Todo>>(items)
    val list: StateFlow<List<Todo>> = _list

    fun add(t: Todo) {
        items.add(t)
        _list.value = items          // "triggers update"
    }
}
// UI
vm.list.map { it.sortedBy(Todo::due) }.distinctUntilChanged().collect(adapter::submitList)

Unit tests with 1 item pass. Release notes mention RecyclerView 1.3 upgrade (red herring). Crash-free rate is 99.9%.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the UI not update, and how do you fix it robustly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames RecyclerView/DiffUtil, or calls notifyDataSetChanged. Misses that StateFlow itself drops the "new" value.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is _list initial and updated value the same object? Does rotation fix it (new collection reads current value)? Does ListAdapter see a new list instance? Is anything else mutating items?
  2. Immediate mitigation: _list.value = items.toList() (hotfix, copy per update).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StateFlow equality: items == items same reference so it is "no change" and not emitted; (b) UI side distinctUntilChanged also drops; (c) submitList with the same instance is ignored by ListAdapter; (d) RecyclerView bug (unlikely).
  4. How I'd verify each: Turbine on vm.list after add: no item emitted. Log System.identityHashCode. Notice that rotation re-subscribes and reads .value, which explains the "fix on rotate".
  5. Root cause: Mutating a list in place and assigning the same instance. MutableStateFlow.value = compares using equals; the same reference is equal to itself so nothing is published. Same reason distinctUntilChanged would drop it, and submitList(sameInstance) is a no-op.
  6. Fix: treat state as immutable:
private val _list = MutableStateFlow<List<Todo>>(emptyList())
fun add(t: Todo) = _list.update { it + t }     // new list, atomic

Short-term the toList() copy; long-term immutable state with update {}, a kotlinx.collections.immutable PersistentList for large lists, or Room as the source of truth. 7. Prevention: Types: expose List, not MutableList; lint rule or code review for "mutable collection inside state"; test that add produces an emission; use ImmutableList/@Immutable in Compose. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not forcing emission with a counter or SharedFlow hack (hides the model bug). Copy-on-write is O(n) per update: fine for hundreds of items, use persistent collections or Room for thousands.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did unit tests with one item pass? -> They asserted on .value after add, which reads the mutated shared list; no emission check.
  • Would distinctUntilChangedBy { it.size } help? -> It hides bugs when contents change at equal size; wrong.
  • Does update {} fix thread safety? -> Yes, CAS-loop; the lambda may be re-run so keep it pure.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "selected items" set mutated in place made the "Select all" button appear dead until the activity recreated. The same stale-reference issue existed in three other screens.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the adapter or calls notifyDataSetChanged.
  • Hire: explains same-reference equality and copies the list.
  • Strong hire: immutable state, update, test for emissions, and cost discussion for large lists.

questions.contextHtml: A trading-lite app (180k DAU) must show "price in the user's currency". Prices tick about 10 times per second per symbol; FX rates arrive about once a minute. A developer wrote price.zip(fxRate) { p, r -> p * r } and QA says: "the displayed price updates only once a minute and is always behind". The product manager's spec says only: "combine the price with the FX rate". Memory is fine, no crashes; the websocket is healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, propose the right operator, and say what clarifying questions you would ask the PM before changing it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "zip and combine are the same" or increases buffer sizes to "speed up" zip.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What should happen when FX is stale (older than N minutes) - show, grey out, or hide? Should each price tick be shown with the latest known FX (yes?) or only paired? What is the initial value before the first FX arrives (block, show USD)? Is it ok to drop intermediate ticks for the UI (60 fps vs 10 Hz)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Swap to combine, ship as hotfix. Behavior is a pure improvement for display.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) zip pairs by index so output rate = slower stream; (b) price flow is being backpressured by zip (the fast side suspends waiting for FX), so the socket buffer grows; (c) FX endpoint is slow (no, one per minute is by design).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log timestamps in the zip transform: one output per FX emission. Memory/Network profiler: socket reads stall or queue. A Turbine test with a virtual clock emitting 10 prices per FX.
  5. Root cause: zip is index-aligned: the n-th price pairs with the n-th FX. Price #1 pairs with FX #1; price #2 waits for FX #2, a minute later. The result is a minute-long lag that grows, since the fast producer is suspended and the pairing falls ever further behind real time.
  6. Fix:
val shown: Flow<Money> = price
    .combine(fxRate.onStart { emit(lastKnownFx ?: 1.0) }) { p, r -> p * r }
    .sample(100)                                  // optional: cap UI work at 10 Hz
    .distinctUntilChanged()

Add a staleness policy from the PM answer (e.g., fxRate flow carries a timestamp; map to a "stale" flag). 7. Prevention: Rule of thumb in review: "state from latest values -> combine; matched pairs of events (request/response, two parallel results for the same input) -> zip". Unit test with different rates. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not zipping with conflate() on both sides to "fix" it - the result is non-deterministic pairing. combine can skip intermediate combos under fast updates, acceptable for display, not for ledgers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When is zip right? -> Pairing results of two independent calls for the same request, e.g., flow1.zip(flow2) of paged data by index, or interleaving with a ticker for pacing.
  • What if FX is a StateFlow? -> combine works the same, and the value is available immediately, no onStart needed.
  • Money calc with Double? -> Use BigDecimal/Long minor units; not a Flow problem but an interviewer favorite.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "live location + geofence list" feature used zip and lagged by minutes; the fix to combine also revealed the geofence stream had never emitted for users without geofences (first-emission rule).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot distinguish zip and combine.
  • Hire: explains index alignment, switches to combine with initial value.
  • Strong hire: asks about staleness and rate, adds sample/distinct, notes combine's conflation and precision concerns.

questions.contextHtml: A fitness app records accelerometer samples at 50 Hz and forwards a "current cadence" metric to a Compose UI and a cloud sync. A dev added .debounce(500) to reduce UI load; now the cadence widget is blank while the user runs and only updates when they stop. Before the change, the UI recomposed 50 times per second and p95 frame time on a Galaxy A13 was 31 ms (jank), battery drain reported at 9%/hour for the feature. The cloud sync also sends one request per sample (50 req/s) and was throttled by the backend.
questions.promptHtml: Fix the pipeline so UI and sync are both sensible, and justify your operator choices.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps debounce but lowers the timeout to 10 ms; or removes the throttling and optimizes recomposition only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What UI refresh is perceptually enough (probably 2-4 Hz for cadence)? Does sync need every sample or aggregates? Is losing the last second of data acceptable on process death? Sensor is registered with which delay (SENSOR_DELAY_GAME = 20 ms)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace debounce(500) with sample(250) for the UI path so it shows a value 4 times per second.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) debounce restarts on every sample (20 ms gap < 500 ms), so it never fires during motion: starvation; (b) UI jank came from 50 recompositions/s; (c) sync needs batching, not sampling; (d) sensor rate itself too high.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log emissions at the collector: none while moving. Layout Inspector recomposition counts; Perfetto frame timeline; Battery Historian; server-side request rate dashboard.
  5. Root cause: Misusing a quiet-period operator on a stream that is never quiet.
  6. Fix:
val cadence: Flow<Float> = sensorSamples()            // 50 Hz callbackFlow
    .map(::computeCadence)
    .distinctUntilChanged()

val ui = cadence.sample(250)                          // 4 Hz, steady, latest value
val sync = cadence
    .runningWindow(size = 100)                        // custom: batch of 100 (2 s)
    .onEach { api.upload(it) }                        // 0.5 req/s instead of 50

where batching is a small custom operator (see the custom operator question) or a scan bucket. Reduce the sensor rate where product allows (SENSOR_DELAY_UI is about 66 ms; the exact value is device-dependent, so measure). 7. Prevention: Operator selection guide in the team doc ("typing: debounce; high-rate: sample; first-click: throttleFirst; batches: custom"). Macrobenchmark with frame timing on a low-end device for any hot flow. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: sample drops intermediate samples, fine for display, not for computing exact aggregates: compute the cadence from the full stream before sampling. I would not use conflate() alone for the UI because it does not cap the rate, only avoids queueing. Upload batching risks losing up to 2 s on process death; persist locally if that matters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the last value before stop must be shown? -> sample can drop the last item after the final tick when the flow completes; use onCompletion to emit the last value or a custom operator.
  • Why not buffer(CONFLATED)? -> It decouples producer/consumer but the consumer still wakes up for every value it can keep up with.
  • How do you test it? -> runTest with advanceTimeBy, emit 50 items per virtual second, assert 4 outputs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scroll analytics event used debounce(100) and showed near-zero events for heavy scrollers, who were exactly the users the team cared about. The fix was sample(1000) plus a final flush on stop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shortens debounce timeout, no understanding of starvation.
  • Hire: switches to sample for the UI and batching for network.
  • Strong hire: computes before sampling, discusses last-value loss, sensor rate/battery, persistence on process death, and testing with virtual time.

questions.promptHtml: How does flatMapMerge limit concurrency, what is the default, and how does it interact with backpressure, ordering and failure? How would you size it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know the API from people who know it as a concurrency primitive, equal to a bounded worker pool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flatMapMerge(concurrency) collects the upstream and launches each inner flow in a child coroutine, using a semaphore to cap how many run at once. The default is 16 (DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, tunable via the kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency system property). When the cap is reached the upstream is suspended, which is natural backpressure. Output order is arrival order, and one inner failure cancels everything. I size it by the scarcest resource: memory per item, connection pool, or server rate limit, not by CPU count."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rough internals (ChannelFlowMerge):

upstream.collect { item ->
    semaphore.acquire()           // suspends upstream when `concurrency` inners are active
    launch { transform(item).collect { send(it) }; semaphore.release() }
}
results flow through a channel (buffered, default 64) to the downstream collector

Consequences:

  • Because it is a ChannelFlow, inner flows run in coroutines launched in the collector's context (the dispatcher of the collecting scope unless flowOn upstream). Use flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) or make the inner flow switch context to parallelize across threads. If the context is Main and the work is a blocking call, concurrency is an illusion.
  • Concurrency of 1 is equal to flatMapConcat semantically (ordered), but implemented through the channel machinery; just use flatMapConcat.
  • concurrency must be positive.
  • Exceptions: first failure cancels siblings and the upstream, then propagates.
  • Cancellation of the collector cancels all inners.
  • The output buffer is separate from the concurrency limit. A slow collector fills the channel (64 by default) and then inner coroutines suspend in send, so you effectively have concurrency items in flight plus 64 buffered results: memory math matters for large payloads.

Sizing: For downloads, an OkHttp Dispatcher has maxRequests = 64 and maxRequestsPerHost = 5 by default, so concurrency above 5 per host just queues in OkHttp. For decode/upload of bitmaps, the limit is heap: N * bytesPerItem, e.g., 12 MP photo decoded = 4000 x 3000 x 4 B = 48 MB each; with a 256 MB heap you can afford 2-3, not 16.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
files.asFlow()
    .flatMapMerge(concurrency = 3) { f ->
        flow { emit(uploader.upload(f)) }       // each upload is one inner flow
    }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .collect { progress.update(it) }

// per-key ordering alternative: serialize with a Mutex per key, or flatMapConcat for global order

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving the default of 16 for memory-heavy work.
  • Expecting results in input order. Tag results with the index if order matters, then sort/buffer.
  • Throwing in one inner flow and losing the other 15 in-flight results.
  • Blocking calls inside the inner flow without Dispatchers.IO; the semaphore is fine, the threads are not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. flatMapMerge vs map { async { } }.awaitAll()? -> The latter starts all at once and is not streaming; flatMapMerge bounds in-flight work and streams results.
  2. How to isolate failures per item? -> catch/runCatching inside the inner flow and emit a Result.
  3. Per-key ordering with global parallelism? -> No groupBy in Flow; use a per-key Channel/actor, or Mutex map, or flatMapMerge on keys with flatMapConcat inside each key's items.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "merge runs in parallel". Senior gives the default, semaphore + channel internals, memory math for in-flight plus buffer, dispatcher caveat and failure/ordering contracts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-upload feature with default concurrency OOMed low-end devices; setting concurrency to 3 dropped the OOM crash rate from 2.1% to 0.1% of upload sessions (see the incident scenario in this chunk).

questions.promptHtml: How does flatMapLatest actually cancel the previous inner flow? What does "cancellation is cooperative" imply for it, and what are the subtleties with buffering?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many people use it daily without knowing that cancellation is cooperative and ordered, so they get stuck pipelines or surprising delays.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flatMapLatest is transformLatest { emitAll(transform(it)) }. It collects the upstream in one coroutine and runs each transform block in a child job. When a new upstream item arrives it cancels the previous child and waits for it to finish cancelling before starting the new one. Because cancellation is cooperative, an inner block that never reaches a suspension point or ignores cancellation delays the next one. The operator is channel based, so it has an internal buffer, and results of a cancelled block that were already sent can still reach the collector."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
upstream item n  ---> cancel(previousJob); join(previousJob); previousJob = launch { block(n) }
block(n):  emitAll(inner(n))  -> send into the ChannelFlow's channel -> downstream collector

Implications:

  1. Cooperative: the cancellation signal (a CancellationException) is delivered at the next suspension point or ensureActive(). A CPU loop or blocking IO (InputStream.read) in the inner flow does not cancel quickly. OkHttp/Retrofit suspend calls do cancel the underlying Call; a blocking JDBC call does not.
  2. Join before start: the new block starts after the old one has completed its cancellation, including finally blocks and NonCancellable cleanup. A slow finally delays the new request.
  3. Buffering: it is a ChannelFlow fused with buffer semantics (default BUFFERED, 64). A cancelled block's already-queued emissions may still be delivered; only emissions after the cancel are prevented. If you need strict "never show stale", tag results with the request key and filter, or use mapLatest + state keyed by query.
  4. Upstream not slowed: upstream is collected in its own coroutine and is never suspended by the inner flow (unlike concat), so a hot upstream produces cancellations at its own rate.
  5. Context: inners run in the collector's context; use flowOn upstream of the operator for upstream work, and withContext/flowOn inside the inner for IO.
  6. Opt-in: @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun results(q: Flow<String>) = q.transformLatest { text ->
    emit(UiState.Loading)
    emit(UiState.Content(api.search(text)))   // cancelled if a new `text` arrives
}
// Bad: non-cooperative inner
q.flatMapLatest { flow { emit(blockingCpuHeavy(it)) } }   // old one runs to completion, new one waits
// Better: make the work cooperative
q.flatMapLatest { flow { emit(withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { heavy(it) /* with ensureActive() checks */ }) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping side-effecting writes in it (cancellation = partial work).
  • Assuming immediate cancel for blocking work.
  • Catching CancellationException inside the inner block and continuing: the join then waits forever or the zombie emits stale data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. flatMapLatest vs collectLatest? -> Former transforms and emits downstream; latter is a terminal that restarts the collector body on each item.
  2. Does a new item arriving while the previous inner is in finally get dropped? -> No, upstream is collected independently; the latest item waits and starts once the previous finishes cancelling; very rapid items effectively collapse because each cancels the pending one.
  3. How do you test the cancel? -> Fake repo with try { awaitCancellation() } finally { cancelled = true } and assert after emitting twice.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "cancels the old one". Senior: cooperative semantics, join-before-start, channel buffering and stale-result risk, and non-idempotent writes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen showed results for the previous query for ~200 ms because a Room-backed inner flow had already queued a result; tagging results by query fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: There is no built-in throttleFirst. Implement one, explain its semantics versus debounce and sample, and discuss testing.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests your ability to write a correct custom operator, choose a time source, and reason about use cases (button clicks).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "throttleFirst(window) emits the first item, drops everything for the window duration, then accepts the next item. I implement it with flow { }, collecting the upstream and tracking a monotonic time mark; no extra coroutines needed. I use a monotonic clock, not wall-clock, and for tests I inject a TimeSource so virtual time works."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Semantics (window = 300 ms; items at 0, 100, 200, 400, 450):

throttleFirst: 0, 400        (0 passes; 100/200 dropped; 400 is >= 300 after 0, passes; 450 dropped)
debounce(300): 450-ish only  (waits for quiet: latest wins, delayed)
sample(300):   latest at each tick

The first item is immediate (zero latency), which is why this is the right choice for click protection, with no trailing delivery.

import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.TimeSource
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

fun <T> Flow<T>.throttleFirst(
    window: Duration,
    timeSource: TimeSource.WithComparableMarks = TimeSource.Monotonic,
): Flow<T> = flow {
    var last: ComparableTimeMark? = null
    collect { value ->
        val l = last
        if (l == null || l.elapsedNow() >= window) {
            last = timeSource.markNow()
            emit(value)
        }
    }
}

Notes: collect inside flow {} keeps context preservation and exception transparency; state (last) is per collection. Time is only compared when an item arrives, so there are no timers/coroutines. TimeSource.Monotonic is not affected by runTest virtual time; in tests use testScheduler.timeSource (available on TestScope as testTimeSource in recent kotlinx-coroutines-test) or inject a fake TimeSource. ComparableTimeMark requires Kotlin 1.9+ stdlib (stable in 1.9); on older versions use TimeMark or System.nanoTime() from SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() on Android.

Usage: clicks.throttleFirst(500.milliseconds).collect { navigate() }. In Android UI, many teams implement the same inside a debounced click listener; flow-based keeps it testable.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• System.currentTimeMillis(): changes with clock adjustments.
  • Implementing with launch/delay inside flow {} -> breaks context invariants.
  • Sharing the window state in a class field -> cross-collector leaks.
  • Expecting trailing value: that is throttleLatest, a different operator (emit first, then the latest at window end).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would throttleLatest differ? -> Emits the first immediately, then at the window end emits the latest suppressed one (needs a timer: channelFlow/conflate with delay).
  2. Why not debounce for click protection? -> It delays the action by the timeout and fires after the last click.
  3. Thread-safety? -> Each collection is sequential; no extra synchronization needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: copies a snippet using currentTimeMillis. Senior: monotonic time, per-collection state, no extra coroutines, testability with injectable time, and relates it to throttleLatest/debounce/sample.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-tap on "Pay" opened two payment sheets on slow devices; a first-wins throttle on the click flow fixed it, plus server-side idempotency.

questions.promptHtml: What rules must a custom Flow operator follow, and what breaks if you violate them? Write a chunked(size) operator as an example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of context preservation and exception transparency - the invariants that make Flow composable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A custom operator should be built with flow { collect { emit } } or transform, so that it emits only from the collector's own coroutine. Rules: preserve context (never emit from another coroutine or dispatcher; use channelFlow if concurrency is needed), keep exception transparency (never catch exceptions that come from emit, i.e. the downstream), be cancellation-friendly (don't swallow CancellationException), and keep state local to the collection. I write chunked with a local buffer and a flush after the upstream completes."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The contract:

  1. Context preservation: the emitting coroutine must be the one that called collect. Violation throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated (emission from another coroutine is detected by SafeCollector).
  2. Exception transparency: a downstream exception thrown inside emit must propagate through the operator. try { emit(x) } catch (e: Exception) { ... } swallows downstream failure and later emission may throw "Flow exception transparency is violated".
  3. Cancellation: do not catch CancellationException; clean up in finally/onCompletion.
  4. Local state: declare mutable state inside the flow { } lambda.
  5. Concurrency needs channelFlow/callbackFlow, which are the sanctioned way to emit from multiple coroutines (via send).
fun <T> Flow<T>.chunked(size: Int): Flow<List<T>> {
    require(size > 0)
    return flow {
        var buf = ArrayList<T>(size)
        collect { v ->
            buf.add(v)
            if (buf.size == size) { emit(buf); buf = ArrayList(size) }  // new list: don't mutate emitted one
        }
        if (buf.isNotEmpty()) emit(buf)       // flush tail on normal completion
    }
}

// BROKEN: violates invariants
fun <T> Flow<T>.badDelayed(): Flow<T> = flow {
    coroutineScope { collect { v -> launch { delay(100); emit(v) } } }  // emit from another coroutine
}
// BROKEN: swallows downstream failure
fun <T> Flow<T>.badSafe(): Flow<T> = flow { collect { try { emit(it) } catch (e: Exception) { /* hide */ } } }

Prefer composing existing operators over writing new ones; transform and channelFlow cover most needs. Note the tail flush above does not run if the upstream fails (exception propagates) - intentional; use onCompletion + care if you want a flush on failure.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Emitting the same mutable list instance and then clearing it: downstream operators like buffer see the cleared list.
  • Using withContext around emit: forbidden (use flowOn).
  • Time-based chunking (size or timeout) needs channelFlow and a timer coroutine.
  • Forgetting require on arguments (trust-boundary check).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make chunked(size, timeout)? -> channelFlow with a collector coroutine that appends under a Mutex and a ticker that flushes, both sending.
  2. Why does flow{} + launch{ emit } fail but channelFlow + launch{ send } works? -> flow checks the emitting coroutine; channelFlow funnels through a channel read by the collector.
  3. How do you test a custom operator? -> Turbine or toList() in runTest; test upstream error, cancellation (assert finally ran), and empty input.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes operators using launch. Senior states the two invariants, knows the error messages, uses channelFlow deliberately and tests failure/cancellation paths.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An in-house bufferTime operator emitted from a timer coroutine inside flow{}, crashing only in release builds when a certain path executed; the fix was channelFlow.

questions.contextHtml:
A notes app (900k DAU) autosaves drafts. Since a refactor, support sees "my last paragraph disappeared" on about 3% of long editing sessions, with no crash. Server logs show the draft endpoint receiving requests whose body is truncated relative to the final text, and some requests with client-side cancellation (499). Code:

private val edits = MutableSharedFlow<Draft>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)

init {
    edits
        .debounce(400)
        .flatMapLatest { draft ->
            flow {
                api.saveDraft(draft.id, draft.text)   // suspend POST
                emit(SaveState.Saved(draft.id))
            }.onStart { emit(SaveState.Saving) }
        }
        .onEach { _saveState.value = it }
        .launchIn(viewModelScope)
}

Typical typing bursts have pauses of 300-1200 ms; mobile p95 request latency is 900 ms on 3G-class networks. The team suspects the server (red herring) and debounce.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, why only on slow networks and long sessions, and how do you redesign the save pipeline?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases debounce, adds retry, or blames the backend. Does not connect request cancellation to flatMapLatest on a write.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are writes idempotent / versioned? Does the server apply a request even if the client cancelled (it may have processed the body already)? Is the order of saves guaranteed server-side? What are the acceptable data-loss semantics (last-write-wins)? What does the 499 rate look like vs slow-network cohort?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace flatMapLatest with flatMapConcat (or mapLatest is equally wrong); ship via staged rollout; add a server ETag/version. Also flush on onCleared/onStop.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) flatMapLatest cancels an in-flight POST when the next draft arrives (typing pause < request latency); the cancelled request may or may not have been committed, and the client state says Saving forever or Saved for the wrong draft; (b) out-of-order arrival of two writes server-side; (c) debounce too short; (d) server bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate client logs (request ids) with server 499 counts per cohort; reproduce with a network-conditioner throttling to 400 kbps and a Turbine test using a fake API with delay(1000) that records cancellation (awaitCancellation + finally); Charles/Proxyman trace.
  5. Root cause: flatMapLatest is "latest wins and cancel the rest". For reads this is correct, since the stale result is worthless. For a write, cancelling means the user's earlier edits may be applied, partially applied, or lost with an unknown state, and the UI shows Saved for a draft id that was never confirmed. On slow networks, the latency (900 ms) exceeds typing pauses (400-1200 ms), so cancellations happen constantly.
  6. Fix: short-term flatMapConcat with conflate() upstream so that at most one save is in flight and the latest text is always the next one:
edits
    .conflate()                       // intermediate drafts collapse while a save is in flight
    .debounce(400)
    .flatMapConcat { d ->
        flow {
            val r = retrying(maxAttempts = 3) { api.saveDraft(d.id, d.text, baseVersion = d.version) }
            emit(SaveState.Saved(r.version))
        }.onStart { emit(SaveState.Saving) }
         .catch { emit(SaveState.Failed(it)) }
    }
    .onEach { _saveState.value = it }
    .launchIn(viewModelScope)

Long-term: persist drafts locally first (Room), sync with WorkManager (survives process death), send full-state PUT with a version for idempotency, and flush on lifecycle stop. 7. Prevention: Rule: "latest-wins operators only for idempotent reads". Test with a fake that records cancellations. Metric: unsaved-draft age and 499 rate. Review checklist item for flatMapLatest, mapLatest, collectLatest containing writes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: NonCancellable around the POST would keep the request, but then you accumulate concurrent writes that can land out of order. Do not just lengthen debounce: the delay hides the bug on fast networks and costs data on app kill. Concat adds latency (queueing) but with conflate the queue length is at most one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user closes the app mid-save? -> The viewModelScope is cancelled; need WorkManager or at least a local persisted draft.
  • Why not collectLatest? -> Same cancellation semantics for the body.
  • Could you keep flatMapLatest and make the server idempotent? -> It helps against duplicates but cancellation still loses the confirmation the client needs; serialize on the client anyway.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "like" button used mapLatest; fast toggling cancelled the first request after the server had applied it, so the client's final state was the opposite of the server's. Lesson: cancellation is not rollback.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bumps debounce, retries, blames server.
  • Hire: identifies cancellation of writes and switches to concat.
  • Strong hire: conflate + version/idempotency, offline-first persistence, process-death handling, and a test that observes cancellation.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app (2.5M DAU) lets users attach up to 40 photos from the gallery; many are 12 MP (4000 x 3000). A new "faster uploads" release processes them as:

photos.asFlow()
    .flatMapMerge { uri -> flow { emit(upload(compress(decode(uri)))) } }
    .collect { progress.advance() }

After release, Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError at BitmapFactory.decodeStream, concentrated on devices with a 256 MB heap limit and 3 GB RAM; crash-free sessions dropped from 99.6% to 97.5% for the attach-photos flow. Logcat excerpt: Throwing OutOfMemoryError "Failed to allocate a 48000012 byte allocation with ... free bytes". Upload bandwidth utilization stays about 20% on the same devices. Red herring: the team had also updated Coil.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the OOM from the code, fix it, and describe how you would choose the right parallelism.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set largeHeap" or "catch OutOfMemoryError". Does not notice the unbounded default concurrency of 16.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the heap limit (ActivityManager.memoryClass) on affected devices? Is decode full-size? How many photos per batch (p50, p95)? Are decode and compress on IO or CPU dispatchers? Is the upload speed network bound?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote config to limit the parallelism; hotfix with flatMapMerge(concurrency = 2); ship to 10%, watch OOM rate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 16 concurrent full-size decodes: 16 x 48 MB = 768 MB demand > 256 MB heap; (b) Coil upgrade increased baseline memory (minor); (c) leaked bitmaps (check retention); (d) uploads holding byte arrays in memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android Studio memory profiler heap dump during a 40-photo batch; capture Debug.getNativeHeapAllocatedSize; count concurrent coroutines with the coroutine debug agent/DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() in a debug build; compute 4000 x 3000 x 4 B = 48,000,000 B (matches the 48000012-byte allocation in the log).
